content: Child development stages outline the key milestones in a child's growth and development. These stages provide a detailed understanding of physical, cognitive, motor, language, and social-emotional progressions that occur as a child matures. Infancy (1-12 months) Cognitive Development: By 6-8 months, infants begin to look for fallen objects and engage in simple games like peek-a-boo. They cannot yet comprehend concepts like no or danger. By 8-12 months, they observe people, objects, and activities in their immediate environment and show awareness of distant objects by pointing. Motor Development: Reflexes such as rooting and sucking are well-developed, while the grasp reflex gradually disappears. Infants begin to raise their head and upper body when prone, turn their head side-to-side when supine, and clasp hands above their face. By the end of this period, they can sit without support, crawl, and may start pulling themselves into a standing position. Physical Growth: Infants grow approximately 2.5 cm per month and gain 100-200 g per week. Their respiration rate is 30-40 breaths per minute, and their body temperature ranges from 35.7°C to 37.5°C. Head circumference increases steadily, reflecting ongoing brain growth. Social and Emotional Development: Infants enjoy being held and read to, and they begin to recognize themselves in mirrors. They also start to imitate adult actions during play. Toddlerhood (12-24 months) Physical Growth: Growth slows, with height increasing by 5-8 cm and weight by 130-250 g per month. The anterior fontanel closes by 18 months, and toddlers begin to lose baby fat as they start walking. Motor Development: Toddlers walk unassisted, climb stairs, and enjoy pushing or pulling toys. They can throw balls underhand, unbutton large buttons, and scribble enthusiastically. Cognitive Development: They enjoy object-hiding games and demonstrate an understanding of functional relationships, such as using a spoon in a bowl. They also begin to name everyday objects and show increasing spatial awareness. Language Development: Toddlers use 5-50 words, often accompanied by gestures. They begin to form two-word phrases and follow simple directions. Speech is 25-50% intelligible. Social and Emotional Development: They show signs of empathy, enjoy adult attention, and begin asserting independence. Tantrums may peak during this period, and they often imitate adult activities. Two-Year-Olds Physical Growth: Weight gain averages 1 kg per year, and height increases by 7-13 cm annually. Posture becomes more erect, though the abdomen may still protrude slightly. Motor Development: They can walk around obstacles, climb stairs, and balance momentarily on one foot. Many achieve toilet training, though accidents are still common. Cognitive Development: Eye-hand coordination improves, and they begin to classify objects based on one dimension. They also discover cause-and-effect relationships and recognize familiar people and objects. Language Development: Vocabulary expands to 50-300 words, and they form threeto four-word sentences. Speech becomes 65-70% intelligible, and they begin to use plurals and negatives. Social and Emotional Development: They show empathy, enjoy helping with household chores, and engage in parallel play. They may be possessive of toys and exhibit defiance. Three-Year-Olds Physical Growth: Height increases by 5-8 cm per year, and weight by 1.4-2.3 kg annually. Baby fat disappears, and the abdomen no longer protrudes. Motor Development: They walk up and down stairs using alternating feet, pedal tricycles, and build towers with blocks. They also show improved control of crayons and markers. Cognitive Development: They enjoy stories, recognize missing puzzle parts, and understand concepts like biggest and more. They can rote count to 20 or more. Language Development: Speech is mostly intelligible, and they use expanded noun phrases and verbs with -ing endings. They answer simple what and where questions. Social and Emotional Development: They engage in make-believe play, show affection toward younger children, and begin to understand turn-taking. They may still defend possessions aggressively. Four-Year-Olds Physical Growth: Weight increases by 1.8-2.3 kg per year, and height by 5-6.5 cm annually. The body becomes more proportionate, and baby fat disappears. Motor Development: They hop on one foot, climb playground equipment, and throw balls with improved aim. They also form shapes with clay and thread beads on a string. Cognitive Development: They recognize rhyming words, name uppercase letters, and understand daily sequences. Some begin reading simple books. Language Development: Vocabulary and sentence complexity increase, and they understand concepts like tallest and same. They enjoy wordplay and storytelling. Social and Emotional Development: They participate in group activities, engage in symbolic play, and show affection toward peers. They may have occasional nightmares and fears.
